quests.instruction: Read the line aloud and join the right pair
quests.hint: -ing words are special: they end with a sound made at the back of the mouth. Find that word.
quests.explanation: The -ing ending is a single sound, /ŋ/, made at the back of the mouth. Because the voice never stops, it bridges into 'out' without a pause and without adding a /g/. Try saying 'going out' as one flowing word.
quests.flowRule: Linking after -ing: The -ing ending is the single nasal /ŋ/. It stays voiced and flows into a following vowel, with no pause and no added /g/.

quests.instruction: Spot the linking point
quests.hint: The word before the link ends in -ing. Say it with the next word and feel the back of your tongue.
quests.explanation: Many people say 'waitin'' casually, but either way the nasal at the end carries over into 'in'. Notice that 'in the' cannot link: /n/ meets /ð/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after -ing: The -ing ending is the single nasal /ŋ/. It stays voiced and flows into a following vowel, with no pause and no added /g/.

quests.instruction: Say it aloud: which words join up?
quests.hint: Weather talk. The word that says what the sky is doing ends in a nasal sound. What follows it?
quests.explanation: Weather chat runs on this kind of link. The /ŋ/ of 'raining' keeps humming straight into the vowel of 'outside', which gives the phrase an unbroken rhythm.
quests.flowRule: Linking after -ing: The -ing ending is the single nasal /ŋ/. It stays voiced and flows into a following vowel, with no pause and no added /g/.

quests.instruction: Tap the pair that sounds like one word
quests.hint: /ʃ/ is the quiet 'sh' sound. You can hold it as long as you like, so what comes after it?
quests.explanation: Hold the 'sh' of 'wash' and let it fade into the vowel of 'up'; that is all the link is. Because /ʃ/ is a continuous sound, this is one of the smoothest links to hear.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that flows without a break
quests.hint: Warnings are said fast. Find the 'ch' sound at the end of a word and see what it meets.
quests.explanation: Warnings cannot afford a gap. The 'ch' of 'watch' is released directly into the vowel of 'out', so you hear one burst of sound. Part of the urgency comes from that speed.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Which boundary has no pause?
quests.hint: One adjective ends with the 'j' sound of 'judge'. What word follows?
quests.explanation: Think of the 'j' in 'judge'. 'Large' ends with that sound, /dʒ/, and a vowel-initial word like 'order' simply picks it up, so 'large order' has one flow from start to finish.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Find the smooth connection
quests.hint: The past ending can sound like /t/ even though it is spelled -ed. Say the verb alone and hear what it ends with.
quests.explanation: The -ed in 'asked' is pronounced /t/, and it is easy to lose before a consonant. Before the vowel in 'about' it survives and attaches. 'About you' is not a vowel link, since /t/ meets /j/.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Listen for the connected words
quests.hint: Here -ed is a /d/. Where does that /d/ end up?
quests.explanation: Drop the /d/ and 'I called a taxi' turns into 'I call a taxi', a different tense. Linking the /d/ onto the weak vowel of 'a' keeps the past tense audible without making it sound heavy.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Identify the linked pair
quests.hint: A dinner story. Which past-tense verb is followed by a word that starts with a vowel?
quests.explanation: The /t/ in 'cooked' is the part that carries the past tense, and here it flows into the opening vowel of 'everything'. Later, 'everything herself' meets /ŋ/ and /h/, which do not link.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken continuously?
quests.textToSpeak: put the book on the shelf
quests.hint: Your eye will want to split every word. Scan for the only place where a consonant sound is followed by a vowel sound.
quests.explanation: Scan for consonant + vowel and you find one place: the /k/ of 'book' meeting 'on'. Every 'the' starts with a consonant, so none of those boundaries can link.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken as one smooth unit?
quests.hint: A family member's name for 'father' ends in a stop. What does the next word begin with?
quests.explanation: Family words link like any other. The /d/ of 'dad' is released into the vowel of 'asked', so 'dad asked' lands as one beat.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which pair would sound choppy if you stopped between them?
quests.hint: Even the tiniest verb joins in. Check the noun before it.
quests.explanation: 'Is' is one of the first words to lose its identity. The /s/ at the end of 'class' lands on the vowel of 'is', which is why listeners who wait for a clearly separate 'is' miss it.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which two words run together?
quests.hint: Questions often begin with a helper verb followed by a short pronoun. See what happens to the helper's last sound.
quests.explanation: In fast speech 'would' is nearly swallowed. Its /d/ then lands on the vowel of 'it', and the start of the question sounds like one word.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the natural transition
quests.hint: Names that begin with a vowel link like any other word. Check what comes before.
quests.explanation: A name that starts with a vowel is easy to treat as a separate unit, but fluent speakers do not. The /d/ of 'did' flows right into the /æ/ of 'Anna'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that blends into one chunk
quests.hint: Look near the end of the question for a short action word followed by a vowel.
quests.explanation: In an invitation, speed signals friendliness. 'Head' ends in /d/ and 'out' begins with /aʊ/, so the /d/ is released into the vowel. 'Shall we' cannot link: /l/ meets /w/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Spot the linking point
quests.hint: Say this instruction the way a receptionist would, in one breath.
quests.explanation: Receptionists say this on autopilot, so it flows. The /t/ of 'wait' is released straight into the vowel of 'outside' instead of being held, so the instruction sounds relaxed rather than curt.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Say it aloud: which words join up?
quests.hint: A dentist or doctor says this. Which verb runs into the next word?
quests.explanation: 'Open' ends in /n/ (often just a syllabic /n/) and 'up' begins with /ʌ/, so the nasal glides in. Soft instructions at a dentist rely on smoothness: the less the speaker stops, the calmer it sounds.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which pair would a fluent speaker say in one breath?
quests.hint: Imagine helping someone with a suitcase. Which action word ends in a hard sound before a weak vowel?
quests.explanation: A request is friendlier without gaps. The /k/ of 'pack' goes directly into the weak /ə/ of 'a', and the stress lands on 'jacket'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that flows without a break
quests.hint: In a longer sentence the link can sit in the middle. Check each word that ends in a consonant.
quests.explanation: In a longer sentence the link hides in the middle, between a verb and its adverb. 'Closes' ends in a /z/ that flows into 'early'; the other boundaries each have a consonant on one side, so they stay separate.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which boundary has no pause?
quests.hint: A word beginning with a weak 'uh' sound is easy to miss. Which one is here?
quests.explanation: The sneaky part is 'along': its first vowel is weak, so you barely hear where the word starts. The /z/ of 'moves' covers that start and the two words run together.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which words melt together when you say this naturally?
quests.hint: A noun and the shortest verb in English. Where do they meet?
quests.explanation: Noun + 'is' is among the most common links in English, and it hides because 'is' is short. The /n/ of 'phone' carries straight into /ɪ/. 'Is nearly' cannot link: /z/ meets /n/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Skip the tempting boundary and find the real link
quests.hint: 'Sit down' sounds like it could link. Check whether the second word begins with a vowel.
quests.explanation: 'Down' ends in /n/ and 'on' begins with a vowel, so they link. 'Sit down' only looks tempting: /t/ meets /d/, two consonants, so there is nothing to flow into.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Identify the linked pair
quests.hint: One word ends in the -ing sound. Check what follows it.
quests.explanation: Two things look linkable here: 'stop talking' and 'talking and'. Only the second has a vowel waiting. The /ŋ/ keeps the voice going into the weak 'and', while 'stop talking' goes /p/ + /t/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after -ing: The -ing ending is the single nasal /ŋ/. It stays voiced and flows into a following vowel, with no pause and no added /g/.

quests.instruction: Read the line aloud and join the right pair
quests.hint: Your ear will want to chop this into separate words. Which two refuse to be chopped?
quests.explanation: The 'ch' of 'check' is released straight into 'on', so the pair is heard as one unit. Nothing else in this sentence has a consonant followed by a vowel, so the link is easy to find once you ignore every 'the'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken as one smooth unit?
quests.hint: A word beginning with a weak vowel often hides a link. See which one this sentence offers.
quests.explanation: 'Away' starts with a weak vowel, so it has almost no edge of its own. The /t/ of 'went' fills the gap and the pair is heard as one. 'Away for' does not link, because the vowel meets /f/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which pair would sound choppy if you stopped between them?
quests.hint: A contraction makes the first word very short. What does its last sound meet?
quests.explanation: Contractions like 'he's' are only one sound long, so there is hardly any time between them and the next word. The /z/ glides into the /ɔː/ of 'already'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Tap the pair that sounds like one word
quests.hint: Contractions are quick. Check what the first word's final sound meets.
quests.explanation: Because 'I'm' is so short, the link is over in a flash: the lips close for /m/ and the voice carries straight into 'also'. Listen for the hum rather than for a gap.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the natural transition
quests.hint: The first word of the pair ends in two consonants. What survives at the end when you say it fast?
quests.explanation: Two consonants close the first word. Whether you say the /d/ lightly or fully, the final consonant of 'stand' flows into the weak vowel starting 'aside'. 'Need to' does not link: /d/ + /t/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that blends into one chunk
quests.hint: Questions beginning with 'what's' flow fast. Find the contraction's neighbour.
quests.explanation: In short questions, linking does much of the rhythmic work. 'What's' ends in /s/ and 'inside' begins with /ɪ/, so the question runs on with the stress falling on 'side'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Find the smooth connection
quests.hint: Tell this as a story, without breaks. Which past-tense verb runs into the next word?
quests.explanation: Telling a story at speed, you would never pause between 'rained' and 'all'. The /d/ stays in, which keeps the past tense audible, and it goes straight into the vowel.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.
